ai.literal: Glory it will yield, wealth also it will yield; than virtue beyond, what gain indeed is there to a soul?
ai.translation: Virtue yields heavenly glory and yields earthly wealth; what greater gain is there for a soul than such virtue?
ai.modern: அறம் ஒருவருக்குச் சிறப்பையும் தரும், செல்வத்தையும் தரும்; ஆதலால், அந்த அறத்தை விட மேலான நன்மை உயிர்களுக்கு வேறு என்ன இருக்க முடியும்?
ai.explanation: The couplet emphasizes the supreme value of virtue in human life. It states that practicing virtue brings both spiritual glory and material wealth. The author poses a rhetorical question, asking what greater benefit or gain can exist for a living being than virtue. The word 'ūuṅku' is an elongated form of 'ūṅku', meaning 'beyond' or 'greater than', which poetically intensifies the comparison. Through this, the couplet establishes virtue as the ultimate source of all well-being.

ai.literal: Than virtue greater gain is not; than forgetting that, greater is not ruin.
ai.translation: There is no greater gain in life than virtue, and there is no greater ruin than forgetting it.
ai.modern: அறத்தை விடச் சிறந்த நன்மை வேறு இல்லை; அந்த அறத்தை மறந்துவிடுவதை விடப் பெரிய கேடு வேறு இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet establishes virtue (அறம்) as the ultimate measure of success and failure in human life. The word 'ஊங்கு' (and its metrically lengthened form 'ஊஉங்கு') means 'beyond' or 'greater than', used here to set absolute boundaries. The poet asserts that no acquisition or prosperity can surpass the value of living virtuously. Conversely, neglecting or forgetting to practice virtue is described as the absolute worst form of ruin that can befall a person.

ai.literal: In the way that is possible, virtuous action, without ceasing, in every opportunity that goes, do.
ai.translation: Perform virtuous deeds without ceasing, in every possible way and at every opportunity.
ai.modern: இயன்ற வழிகளில் எல்லாம் அறச் செயல்களை இடைவிடாமல், அவை செய்யக்கூடிய இடங்கள் மற்றும் வாய்ப்புகள் அனைத்திலும் செய்ய வேண்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the continuous practice of virtue in daily life. The term 'ஒல்லும் வகையான்' means 'by whatever means possible', suggesting that one should not wait for grand circumstances but do whatever small good is within their power. 'ஓவாதே' means 'without ceasing', highlighting that virtue is a constant practice rather than an occasional act. 'செல்லும்வாய் எல்லாம்' refers to every opportunity or place where it is possible to act righteously. Thus, the couplet instructs us to perform good deeds continuously, using every available means and opportunity.

ai.literal: In the mind, being one who is without impurity, that much is virtue; of the nature of empty show are other things.
ai.translation: To be spotless in mind is the entirety of virtue; all else is merely empty, ostentatious show.
ai.modern: மனதில் குற்றம் இல்லாதவனாக இருப்பதே அறம் ஆகும்; மற்றவை எல்லாம் வெறும் ஆரவாரத் தன்மை உடையவை.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the true essence of virtue as internal purity. The poet states that being free from mental impurities (மாசு இலன் ஆதல்) is the complete measure of virtue (அனைத்து அறன்). Any external action or ritual performed without this inner purity is dismissed as mere ostentation or empty noise (ஆகுல நீர பிற). The word 'மனத்துக்கண்' emphasizes that the locus of virtue is the mind, and 'ஆகுல' highlights the loud, showy nature of superficial deeds.

ai.literal: Envy, desire, anger, and harsh words—practicing without slipping from these four is virtue.
ai.translation: Virtue is that which is practiced by consistently avoiding these four: envy, desire, anger, and harsh speech.
ai.modern: பொறாமை, பேராசை, சினம், கடுஞ்சொல் ஆகிய நான்கையும் விலக்கி, தடையின்றிச் செய்யப்படும் செயலே அறம் ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the practical path of virtue by identifying four negative traits that must be completely avoided. These are envy (அழுக்காறு), greed or excessive desire (அவா), anger (வெகுளி), and harsh words (இன்னாச்சொல்). The word 'இழுக்கா' means 'without slipping' or 'without failing', emphasizing that one must consistently avoid these four flaws. True virtue (அறம்) is not just doing good deeds, but conducting one's life in a way that is entirely free from these four destructive qualities.

ai.literal: Without saying 'We will know (and do it) then', do virtue; indeed, that, at the time of perishing, is an imperishable companion.
ai.translation: Do not delay, saying, 'We will practice virtue later.' Do it now, for that virtue will be an imperishable companion when you perish.
ai.modern: ‘பிறகு பார்த்துக் கொள்ளலாம்’ என்று தள்ளிப்போடாமல் அறத்தைச் செய்ய வேண்டும்; அதுவே நாம் அழியும் காலத்தில் அழியாத துணையாக இருக்கும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the urgency of practicing virtue without procrastination. The phrase 'அன்று அறிவாம்' represents the attitude of delaying good deeds to old age or a future time. The author advises doing virtue immediately because when the body perishes ('பொன்றுங்கால்'), only the virtue performed remains as an undying companion ('பொன்றாத் துணை') to support the soul. The contrast between the perishing body and the imperishable companion highlights the eternal value of righteous actions.

ai.literal: The fruit of virtue is this, saying so is not needed; it is seen between the palanquin bearer and the rider.
ai.translation: There is no need to explain the fruit of virtue with words; it is plainly visible in the contrast between the bearer of the palanquin and the one who rides in it.
ai.modern: அறத்தின் பயன் இது என்று நூல்களைக் கொண்டு விளக்க வேண்டியதில்லை; பல்லக்கைத் தூக்கிச் செல்பவனுக்கும் அதில் ஏறிச் செல்பவனுக்கும் இடையே உள்ள வேறுபாட்டிலேயே அது விளங்கும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a vivid, everyday image to illustrate the self-evident nature of the fruits of virtue. The word 'ஆறு' can mean 'path' or 'fruit/result'; in this context, 'fruit' or 'consequence' fits best. The poet argues that one does not need elaborate philosophical arguments to prove the power of virtue. Instead, the stark contrast between the physical toil of the palanquin bearer ('பொறுத்தான்') and the comfort of the rider ('ஊர்ந்தான்') serves as a direct, visible demonstration of how past actions shape present circumstances.

ai.literal: If a person performs virtue without letting wasted days occur, that is a stone that blocks the path of their days of living.
ai.translation: If one performs virtuous deeds daily without letting a single day go to waste, that practice will be a stone that blocks the path of future rebirths.
ai.modern: ஒருவன் வீணான நாள் எதுவும் ஏற்படாதவாறு தினமும் அறச்செயல்களைச் செய்வானானால், அது அவனுடைய பிறவி வழியை அடைக்கும் கல்லாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the importance of daily, uninterrupted practice of virtue. The term 'வீழ்நாள்' refers to a wasted day, which in this context means a day spent without doing any good deeds. The poet suggests that if a person performs virtue ('நன்று') consistently every single day without fail ('படாஅமை'), that continuous practice acts like a heavy stone ('கல்') that blocks ('அடைக்கும்') the path ('வழி') of future births ('வாழ்நாள்'). Here, 'வாழ்நாள்' (literally, days of living) is used to represent the cycle of rebirths, and the blocking stone represents the cessation of this cycle through the power of accumulated virtue.

ai.literal: By virtue that which comes indeed is happiness; other all are external, fame also do not have.
ai.translation: Only that pleasure which flows from a life of virtue is true happiness; all other pleasures are external to it and yield no lasting praise.
ai.modern: அறவழியில் வருவதே உண்மையான இன்பம் ஆகும்; மற்ற வழிகளில் வருவன எல்லாம் இன்பத்திற்குப் புறம்பானவை, அவை புகழையும் தராது.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the true source of happiness as virtue. It asserts that only the joy arising from righteous living is genuine and wholesome. Any other form of pleasure obtained through unrighteous means is described as external, meaning it is superficial, fleeting, and disconnected from the soul. Furthermore, such pleasures do not bring any true or lasting glory to a person.

ai.literal: That which is fit to be done, after considering, is virtue indeed to a person; that which is fit to be avoided, after considering, is blame.
ai.translation: Virtue is that which a person ought to perform, and disgrace is that which one ought to avoid, after careful consideration.
ai.modern: ஒருவன் ஆராய்ந்து செய்யத்தக்கது அறமே ஆகும்; அவன் ஆராய்ந்து விலக்கத்தக்கது பழியே ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet summarizes the essence of a righteous life by defining what must be embraced and what must be shunned. The word 'செயற்பாலது' refers to actions that are duty-bound and proper to perform, which the poet identifies solely as virtue ('அறனே'). Conversely, 'உயற்பாலது' refers to things from which one must escape or avoid, identified here as blame or disgrace ('பழி'). The recurring word 'ஓரும்' suggests careful contemplation or investigation, emphasizing that these choices should not be made blindly but through deliberate discernment.
